enrichment.short_title: MHRT adjournment to hear responsible medical officer
key_facts: Patient X, detained under sections 37 and 41 after serious 1988 offences, applied to the Mental Health Review Tribunal for discharge.
Expert evidence conflicted on whether he still suffered a mental disorder within the meaning of the Act.
After a long hearing the Tribunal adjourned to require attendance and a report from the responsible medical officer, Dr T, who had not produced a report or given evidence.
X sought judicial review, arguing the late adjournment was procedurally unfair and that the Tribunal should decide on the material before it.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a Mental Health Review Tribunal decision to adjourn a discharge application.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the Tribunal's adjournment was held lawful though procedurally flawed, and permission to appeal was refused.
enrichment.ratio: A Mental Health Review Tribunal may adjourn of its own motion under rule 16 to obtain further information where necessary to reach the correct decision, but must invite submissions before adjourning; a breach of procedural propriety does not automatically make the adjournment unlawful if the Tribunal reasonably regarded further evidence from the RMO as necessary in a serious public-interest case.
legal_issues: Whether MHRT proceedings are adversarial or inquisitorial
Power to adjourn after evidence and submissions have concluded
Procedural fairness and Article 5(4) delay
Whether seeking evidence from the RMO was an improper attempt to bolster the hospital's case
index_terms: B v Mental Health Review Tribunal

linked_authorities.name: B v Mental Health Review Tribunal and the Secretary of State
C v London & South West Mental Health Review Tribunal

confidence.notes: Full judgment text with clear reasoning on adjournment powers and procedural fairness.

enrichment.short_title: Section 20B and advance service charge payments
key_facts: Tenants at 27 Lennox Gardens challenged service charge accounting for years ending March 1999 and 2000.
Final accounts were issued in October 2001, more than 18 months after some expenditure was incurred.
Actual expenditure was less than quarterly payments on account, so no balancing demand was made.
Master Price had declared section 20B inapplicable where expenditure was covered by advance service charges.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Chancery Master’s determination of a preliminary issue on section 20B of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Master Price’s construction of section 20B was upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Section 20B applies only where a further demand is required because actual expenditure exceeds payments on account; quarterly on-account payments are themselves service charges within section 18, and the issue of a final certificate and account is not a demand for payment where no balance is outstanding.
legal_issues: Whether section 20B applies to expenditure covered by advance service charge payments
Whether final accounts constitute a demand for payment under section 20B(1)
Interaction of sections 19(2) and 20B
Policy behind the 18-month limitation

confidence.notes: Detailed statutory analysis with clear outcome on a discrete preliminary issue.

enrichment.short_title: Freezing order against Congo refused on notice
key_facts: Kensington held a summary judgment for about US$57m against the Republic of the Congo under a 1984 loan agreement with waived sovereign immunity.
Tomlinson J refused contractual injunctive relief; Kensington then applied ex parte for a Mareva-style freezing order covering Congo oil entities SNPC, SNPC UK and Olearius.
Morison J declined to hear the application without notice and directed inter partes hearing with notice to the Congo and related entities.
The Court of Appeal held Morison J’s discretionary decision could not be impugned on appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a refusal to grant a without-notice freezing injunction pending enforcement of a debt judgment.
enrichment.ratio: Where a creditor seeks a wide freezing order against a foreign state and related oil-trading entities after prior enforcement steps and a contested injunction trial, an appellate court will not interfere with a judge’s decision that justice requires notice and an inter partes hearing unless the decision was one the judge could not reasonably reach.
legal_issues: Whether Mareva relief should be granted ex parte against a foreign sovereign
Risk of asset dissipation in large-scale oil trading structures
Appropriate scope and notice requirements for freezing orders
Relationship between judgment debt enforcement and injunctive relief

confidence.notes: Appellate review of case management/discretion with substantial factual background recited.

enrichment.short_title: OFT competition investigation warrants and human rights
key_facts: The Office of Fair Trading applied without notice for warrants to investigate suspected price-fixing cartel conduct.
Morison J was satisfied there were reasonable grounds to suspect Chapter 1 infringement and that documents might be concealed or destroyed.
The judgment addressed whether compulsory document production and questioning under the warrants infringed Article 6 and Article 8 rights.
Warrants had already been executed when the anonymised judgment was handed down.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Without-notice application for Competition Act 1998 investigation warrants with a published ruling on Human Rights Act compatibility.
enrichment.outcome: Warrants granted; the OFT’s powers were held compatible with Articles 6 and 8 as proportionate safeguards existed.
enrichment.ratio: Competition investigation powers to enter premises, seize documents and ask factual questions pursue a legitimate aim and are proportionate where a High Court judge supervises warrant issue, legal privilege is protected, and answers cannot be compelled where they would amount to an admission of infringement contrary to the Orkem principle.
legal_issues: Article 6 fair trial and privilege against self-incrimination in competition investigations
Whether cartel penalties are criminal for Convention purposes
Article 8 interference with business premises
Comparison with EC Commission investigation guarantees

confidence.notes: Structured human rights analysis; defendant identities deliberately withheld in judgment.

enrichment.short_title: School Sites Act reverter at St Philips Maidstone
key_facts: Land at St Philips School, Maidstone was conveyed in 1866 under the School Sites Act 1841 for a National Society church school.
The school closed in 1995; claimants argued reverter occurred before 17 August 1975 so their title was statute-barred before the 1987 Act.
Evidence showed some pupils from outside the ecclesiastical district and from non-poorer social classes, but most remained qualifying pupils.
The diocesan board argued use had ceased for trust purposes because the school effectively educated all-comers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issue on whether automatic reverter occurred more than twelve years before the Reverter of Sites Act 1987.
enrichment.outcome: Preliminary issue answered in the negative; no reverter before the 1987 Act.
enrichment.ratio: Reverter under section 2 of the School Sites Act 1841 occurs only if land ceases to be used for the purpose stated in the conveyance; educating some non-qualifying pupils alongside a majority of qualifying pupils does not mean the land ceased to be used for the stated purpose, and integration into the state education system did not of itself trigger reverter.
legal_issues: Construction of National Society model trust wording
Whether residence in the ecclesiastical district was required
Distinction between breach of trust and cessation of use
Effect of educating non-poorer-class or out-of-district pupils

linked_authorities.name: Fraser v Canterbury Diocesan Board of Finance
National Society v School Board of London

enrichment.short_title: Green Belt time extension refused ignoring Barn restoration

statutes_considered.title: Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990

key_facts: Outline permission for a golf course, hotel and leisure development at St Clere's Farm in the Green Belt depended on enabling development to fund listed building works.
Section 106 works to St Clere's Hall and to arrest decline of the Barn were largely completed, but Barn restoration was intended as part of the hotel scheme.
The claimant sought under section 73 to extend time to submit reserved matters for the hotel after missing the deadline.
The inspector dismissed the appeal, treating completed section 106 works as removing very special circumstances for Green Belt development.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to an inspector’s dismissal of a section 73 appeal to extend time for reserved matters approval.
enrichment.outcome: Application allowed; the inspector’s decision was quashed for failure to consider Barn restoration as a material consideration.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 73 application to extend time limits, the potential cost and planning importance of restoring a listed Barn as part of an enabling hotel development in the Green Belt is a material consideration distinct from completed section 106 repair works; an inspector who reasons only from the latter may have failed to take into account a relevant factor warranting quashing.
legal_issues: Material change in circumstances since 1995 outline permission
Very special circumstances for inappropriate Green Belt development
Enabling development under English Heritage policy
Whether partial implementation and legitimate expectation supported extension

confidence.notes: Primary ground of success clearly identified; numerous subsidiary grounds addressed briefly.

key_facts: Mr Bhamjee lost planning and enforcement challenges over use of his yard for car washing and related activities from 1999 onwards.
He issued multiple Chancery claims against barristers and the Treasury Solicitor for negligence, human rights breaches and related relief.
Park J struck out the claims as incoherent and dismissed an appeal against Master Bowman’s strike-out of a related insolvency claim.
Brooke LJ granted an extension of time but dismissed the appeal and ordered a stay pending consideration of an injunction to control future litigation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal out of time against strike-out of claims against lawyers and the Treasury Solicitor.
enrichment.outcome: Extension of time granted; appeal dismissed; stay on further applications to the Court of Appeal; judgment sent to civil justice stakeholders.
enrichment.ratio: Barristers conducting litigation owe no duty of care to the opposing litigant (Connolly-Martin v Davis), and repeatedly re-litigating finally determined planning issues through incoherent claims against lawyers is hopeless; the court may also highlight the resource cost of meritless fee-exempt appellate applications.
legal_issues: Whether opposing counsel owe a duty of care after Hall v Simons
Strike-out of incoherent claims
Extension of time to appeal
Control of vexatious or persistent litigants in person

enrichment.short_title: CPR service rules: five consolidated appeals
key_facts: Five pre-Anderton appeals raised recurring problems with serving claim forms within four months and with CPR 6.9 and 7.6.
In Cranfield the court failed to serve issued claim forms through oversight; the Court of Appeal held CPR 7.6(3)(a) covers court neglect.
McManus and Claussen concerned unsuccessful attempts to dispense with service; Murphy held service on a company’s registered office under section 725 was valid.
Smith held service at an individual’s last known residence under CPR 6.5(6) is good service even if the defendant may no longer live there.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated appeals on construction and exercise of CPR powers to extend time for service and dispense with service.
enrichment.outcome: Mixed: Cranfield and Smith appeals allowed; Claussen, McManus and Murphy appeals dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 7.6(3)(a) includes cases where the court failed to serve through neglect; CPR 6.9 may retrospectively dispense with service only in exceptional pre-Anderton category 2 cases where the issued claim form was received by the defendant or authorised solicitor by a permitted method within four months, without circumventing Godwin; service on a company’s registered office under section 725(1) remains an alternative to CPR service.
legal_issues: Meaning of court ‘unable to serve’ under CPR 7.6(3)(a)
Scope of CPR 6.9 after Anderton and Wilkey
Service on insurers rather than defendant or authorised solicitor
Service at last known residence under CPR 6.5(6)
Interaction of Companies Act service and CPR 6.4(2)

enrichment.short_title: Park and Ride mitigation site planning condition

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (General Development Procedure) Order 1995

key_facts: Hampshire County Council obtained outline permission in 1998 for a Park and Ride on Bar End Meadows, restored grassland after the M3 extension at Twyford Down.
Condition 5 required approval of a mitigation scheme on one of five listed replacement chalk grassland sites before development.
The council approved site 7 at Magdalen Hill without reconsidering comparative merits of nearer sites, treating the Secretary of State’s decision as settling principle.
Murray, a nearby resident, judicially reviewed the approval of mitigation details.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against quashing of local planning authority decisions approving mitigation details under a planning condition.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the authority had not erred in treating site choice as constrained by the condition, and section 92 did not limit submission of non-reserved-matter details.
enrichment.ratio: A planning condition requiring one of five named mitigation sites does not incorporate the inspector’s non-binding order of preference; the planning authority need not reopen comparative site merits at the details stage if any listed site can offset ecological loss, and off-site mitigation conditions are not reserved matters subject to section 92’s three-year limit.
legal_issues: Material considerations when approving mitigation details
Whether inspector’s site preference bound the planning authority
Whether mitigation approval was a reserved matter under section 92
Public funding and prompt challenge to later reconsideration

enrichment.short_title: CEO dismissal fair after takeover board removal
key_facts: Mr Cobley was chief executive and director of FTI for nearly 20 years and led a failed management buy-out against Crest’s successful takeover in January 2000.
Shareholders removed him as a director at an EGM; his contract automatically terminated when he ceased to be a director.
The employment tribunal found the reason was some other substantial reason: new owners replacing the board after a hostile takeover battle.
Cobley’s unpaid wages claim succeeded but his unfair dismissal appeal failed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission on questions of law from employment tribunal and EAT decisions on unfair dismissal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; dismissal held fair for some other substantial reason.
enrichment.ratio: Where a chief executive’s contract terminates automatically on removal as director, the substantial reason for dismissal may be the change of control and replacement of the board following a hostile takeover, which can justify dismissal of the chief executive as a potentially fair some other substantial reason if dismissal was within the range of reasonable responses.
legal_issues: Whether change of share ownership is some other substantial reason
Relationship between removal as director and termination of employment
Fairness under section 98(4) where employee anticipated departure
Whether manner of dismissal rendered dismissal unfair

confidence.notes: Full Court of Appeal judgment on established employment law principles with clear facts.
